name: Natural TRT / "enclo + hCG" protocols

card.summary: Non-testosterone ways of raising testosterone, such as enclomiphene and hCG, that aim to avoid shutting down fertility; discussed as TRT alternatives, with limited evidence.
card.note: Enclomiphene is not approved in the US or EU; hCG and SERMs are prescription drugs.

quick.overview:
"Natural TRT" is a community label for approaches that raise the body's own testosterone production instead of replacing it with injected testosterone. The usual examples are enclomiphene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a hormone that stimulates the testes.

The appeal described by proponents is keeping sperm production and testicular function. Medical sources describe hCG and clomiphene-type drugs as alternatives for some men with low testosterone, though evidence for enclomiphene is limited and it never received marketing approval.
quick.mechanism: Enclomiphene blocks estrogen's negative feedback at the pituitary, raising LH and FSH and so the testes' testosterone output. hCG acts on the LH receptor of the testes and stimulates testosterone production without suppressing sperm production, but it cannot work if the testes themselves cannot make testosterone [1][2].
quick.risks: Enclomiphene safety data in 1,403 participants listed headache, hot flush and nausea, with rare thromboembolic events and one fatal stroke. The EU's CHMP recommended refusing authorisation in 2018 and development was discontinued in 2021. Products sold online outside medical supervision are not regulated for quality [1].

lead: "Natural TRT" or "enclo + hCG" refers to protocols in which men aim to raise their own testosterone using drugs that stimulate the pituitary-testicular axis, rather than taking testosterone itself. Enclomiphene (enclomifene) is a nonsteroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator, the more antiestrogenic isomer of clomifene, and hCG is a gonadotropin that mimics LH.[1][2][4]

The appearance case, as proponents put it, runs through testosterone: higher testosterone supports muscle mass, leaner body composition, energy for training, libido and the masculine traits associated with androgen exposure, and doing it through the body's own signalling is meant to preserve testicular size, sperm production and fertility.[3][5] Exogenous testosterone can suppress spermatogenesis, which is why fertility-preserving options are of interest.[3] The hypogonadism article states that hCG stimulates testosterone production without suppressing sperm production and that low-dose clomifene is an alternative to replacement.[2]

In bodybuilding the same logic appears in a different form: hCG is commonly used during and after anabolic steroid cycles to help maintain testicular size and natural testosterone output.[4] On looksmax.org, enclomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-raising compound, alongside threads reporting side effects such as fatigue.[6][7]

chain: Enclomiphene raises LH and FSH; hCG mimics LH at the testes
Higher natural testosterone with fertility signalling kept active
More muscle, leaner body composition and training drive
angle.text: People use these protocols to raise testosterone, which influences muscle mass, body composition and energy for training. The distinguishing feature is that the body's own production is stimulated rather than replaced, with testicular function and fertility intended to stay active.

infobox: EU recommendation to refuse approval 2018; development discontinued 2021 [1]
Raise endogenous testosterone while preserving fertility

paras: Enclomifene is the (E)-stereoisomer of clomifene, which is about 62% enclomifene and 38% zuclomifene; enclomifene is the more antiestrogenic of the two. By blocking estrogen feedback at the pituitary it raises gonadotropin secretion and thereby testicular testosterone production.[1]
In secondary hypogonadism, where LH is low or normal, the testes can respond to gonadotropin stimulation; in primary hypogonadism LH is usually elevated and the testes themselves are impaired.[2]

Human chorionic gonadotropin binds the LH receptor on testicular Leydig cells and stimulates testosterone production, which in turn supports sperm production. It is used medically in some forms of hypogonadism, alone or alongside testosterone, and to treat or prevent infertility including during testosterone replacement, where it helps preserve fertility and prevent testicular atrophy.[4]

In bodybuilding, hCG is commonly used during and after anabolic steroid cycles to maintain testicular size and natural testosterone output.[4] It is on some sports' banned lists, and athletes including baseball's Manny Ramirez (2009) and the NFL's Brian Cushing have been sanctioned after positive tests.[4]

Wikipedia cites a 2013 comparison of oral enclomiphene with testosterone gel that reported maintained sperm counts alongside raised testosterone, and a 2014 study reporting that enclomiphene raised serum testosterone within 14 days in men with low testosterone.[1] Safety data from 1,403 participants in phase 2 and 3 studies listed headache (1.6%), hot flush (1.1%) and nausea (1.0%), with rarer events including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and one fatal ischemic stroke.[1] No published trial of an enclomiphene plus hCG combination was identified.

Enclomiphene was developed as Androxal and EnCyzix for male hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes. It was under FDA and EMA review by December 2016, the EMA's CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorisation in January 2018, and development was discontinued for all indications in April 2021.[1] Clomifene citrate is FDA-approved for ovulatory infertility and male infertility.[1]

Wikipedia describes testosterone replacement as the classic treatment for male hypogonadism, with possible effects on spermatogenesis, hematocrit and sleep apnea.[3] In 2025, after the TRAVERSE trial, the FDA removed a boxed warning for cardiovascular risk from testosterone labels.[3]

On looksmax.org, enclomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-maximising compound; one thread title claims it gives users testosterone in the 90th to 99th percentile, and another is framed as a complete guide to testosterone maxxing.[7][8] Other users report adverse experiences, for example fatigue and sleepiness after taking it.[6] In a thread asking whether enclomiphene could help with height or bones, a reply said it would do little unless testosterone is low and that growth hormone, not testosterone or DHT, is what matters for bone growth.[9]

lore.intro: Enclomiphene and hCG are discussed on looksmax.org as ways to raise testosterone without injecting it, with side-effect reports and sourcing questions appearing alongside enthusiasm.[6][7]

claims.claim: Enclomiphene can push testosterone into the 90th to 99th percentile
claims.believers: A thread title states this outright, and users present it as a strong non-suppressive way to raise testosterone.[7][8]
claims.experts: Trials cited by Wikipedia report raised serum testosterone in men with low testosterone and maintained sperm counts; the drug was not approved in the EU and development was discontinued.[1]

claims.claim: hCG keeps the testes active and fertile
claims.believers: Practitioners say hCG maintains testicular size and natural output during or after steroid use or replacement.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes hCG as stimulating testosterone production without suppressing sperm production, and as used for fertility preservation during testosterone replacement.[2][4]

claims.claim: Enclomiphene may help bone growth or height
claims.believers: Some users ask whether it can aid height or bonemaxxing.[9]
claims.experts: Replies in the thread themselves note that growth hormone rather than testosterone or DHT drives bone growth, and no published trial tests enclomiphene for height.[9]
Clinical trial data list headache, hot flush and nausea, with rare thromboembolic events; one forum user reports feeling fatigued and sleepy after each use.[1][6]
